paragraphs.text: Once the life-giver’s ascension crowned us with fitting and festive crowns, for he raised up our human nature and planted it in heaven. That was the very beginning of the discourse: that the Savior gained every benefit for us. He bestowed nothing on himself, but granted salvation to us. For he made our earthly nature heavenly, and established this earth, food for the grave, as a part of the heavenly natures. For the divine apostle indeed knows how to speak of an earthly image and a heavenly image. And we can hear this in his own words: “The first man,” he says, “came from the earth, earthly; the second man is the Lord from heaven.” And in the same passage he adds: “As is the earthly one, so also are those who are earthly.” “And as is the heavenly one, so also are those who are heavenly.” He does not call the earthly one earthly because he came from the earth, but because he performed earthly deeds. And he calls the heavenly one heavenly not because he had his body from heaven—for he took his body from the Virgin and from the earth—but heavenly because he possessed virtue in himself, and because it was the heavenly one’s body. He did not call it heavenly by nature, but because of the heavenly one who clothed himself in it.

The first man came from the soil and lived by earthly deeds. The dust that rises is called dirt, and what bears fruit is called earth. And so he does not call the man merely a man of the earth, but earthly, having come into the dust of sins. Just as clothes and eyes are harmed by dust, so souls are harmed by sins. Just as clothes and faces become clean when the dust is shaken off, so also, when you cast away your sins, souls become clean and light. As the blessed David also says: “Like arrows in the hand of a mighty man, so are the sons of those who have shaken themselves free.” And as he says of Jerusalem: “Rise and shake your dust off yourself.” The heavens likewise take their form in accordance with the earthly man who is clothed in earthly deeds. When people are stained with sins as though with dust, the heavens also sift down dirt. And there is nothing strange in saying that dust is sifted down from heaven—not because of the nature of heaven, but because of the worthiness of [?]. And who will bear witness to these words? God, through Moses, who said: “If you do not listen to the laws of the Lord your God, your rain will become dust for you, and dirt will descend from heaven.” “If you do not remain in the laws of the Lord your God, your rain will become dust, and dirt will descend from heaven.” And dirt is sifted down upon the earthly man, because he clothed himself in the dust of sins.

And just as he brings forward this example concerning such people—that the heavens will rain dirt upon the earthly man—so also there is something fitting for each person’s will. If he sees a hard mind, he acts according to its hardness; and if a gentle one, according to its gentleness. Indeed, many are hard and rough like iron and bronze. As Isaiah also says of Israel: “I knew that you are hard, and that your neck is an iron sinew and your forehead bronze.” By “an iron sinew” he means the disobedient neck that grows weary and avoids coming under the yoke of worshiping God, recoiling from the laws, according to the saying: “Ephraim became a heifer that cast off the yoke, and did not accept the yoke.” And when people remain in such hardness, disobedience, and unbelief, God also alters creation accordingly. “And if you do not listen to my laws, I will make the heavens above you bronze, and the earth beneath you iron.” This means that he makes it without seed and without fruit.

In accordance with the earthly man, created things likewise take their form to exact vengeance for their evil deeds and their contempt for the Creator’s laws. But whoever bears the likeness of the heavenly one, according to the saying, “Just as we have put on the image of the heavenly one,” the heavens likewise take shape. And upon anyone whose mind is gentle, a rain of sweetness pours down. And because he has fulfilled the divine commandments, he fills his fields with heavenly dew. “Receive,” he says, “the dew of my commandments, and I will bring you the dew of rain.” If our souls are watered with divine commandments, he also waters our fields with beneficial rains. If you listen to the laws of the Lord your God [?], the heavens will give their dew, and the earth its fruit. The earth bears fruit for the obedient.

“From now on, let us put on the image of the heavenly one.” He calls the Savior heavenly, not merely because he is from heaven, for that is already evident, since God the Word is not only heavenly but also Lord of heaven and of the angels. Rather, he is heavenly also according to the flesh, because on earth he practiced the virtue of heaven. For if he calls the Savior heavenly merely because he is from heaven, how does he also call others heavenly, when their nature was not from heaven? Likewise, blessed David calls him heavenly, for I find that name used once in the Old Testament as well as in the New. Paul says, “Let us put on the image of the heavenly one,” and David says, “When the heavenly one separates the kings upon it.” Upon it—upon what? Upon the earth.

And that David applied the word “heavenly” to the Savior, and that this is not a forced interpretation of the words or merely a coincidence of names, but agreement borne out by the truth of the deeds themselves—learn this directly from the sequence of the passage: David calls the Savior heavenly. “When the heavenly one separates them upon it,” he says, “it will snow on Salmon: the mountain of God, a fertile mountain, a great mountain, a fertile mountain.” I will explain the sequence point by point, so that the interpretation of the words may not appear forced, since we apply the name “heavenly” to the Savior. [?] Let the sequence and the words of our discourse proceed clearly and without any muddled confusion. Let no one suppose that this is a forced interpretation, but rather a true correspondence. “When the heavenly one separates the kings upon it,” he says, “they will be covered with snow.” And what does it mean for the heavenly one to separate the kings upon the earth?

Here he calls kings of the earth not those who possess worldly honor, but those whose minds have been illumined by heavenly understanding—the saints, of whom Paul says, “If we suffer, we will also reign with him.” Paul speaks of the kingdom of the saints, not idly with grand words and an excess of honor that makes his listeners proud. For it is often possible to speak extravagantly, to stir the ears of one's listeners by lavishing grand words upon them and draw them toward the matters set before them. But Paul does not deceive by lavishing grand words. Indeed, he is not even able to speak in a manner worthy of the promises. He himself bears witness: “What the eye has not seen, and the ear has not heard, and what has not entered the human heart, God has prepared for those who love him.” A kingdom will be given to the saints—not a worldly kingdom, but the heavenly one, after the likeness of the kingdom that the Savior possesses. When Pilate asked him, “Are you the king of the Jews?” he said, “My kingdom is not of this world. If it were of this world, my servants would fight for me.” A kingdom will be given to the saints, as Paul says, and Daniel agrees with him. “After that,” he says, “God will raise up a great and mighty kingdom, which will stand and remain forever.” And again: “The saints of the Most High will receive the kingdom.” And here he says, “When the heavenly one separates the kings upon it.”

What does “to separate” mean? To distinguish, to divide. How will he distinguish the kings? It is precisely this: having commanded Paul to be a preacher of the kingdom, he sent him as a preacher of the kingdom from Jerusalem as far as the regions of Illyricum. And he sent one to the Indians, another to the regions of the east, another to the regions of the west, another to the south, and the others to the north. In separating—that is, distinguishing and dividing—which people or which person ought to be heeded, and who should listen to whom and believe, he likewise sent the preachers according to what was appropriate for each. “When the Heavenly One separates the kings over it,” he says, “they will become snowy on Zalmon,” that is, they will become white. For the preaching of the apostles made the whole world white and showed the earth to be whiter than snow. For it washed the earth with the word of truth and wiped it clean, according to the saying, “You will wash me, and I will become whiter than snow.” Pay attention to the sequence: “When the Heavenly One separates the kings over it, they will become snowy on Zalmon.” Zalmon is Hebrew and is translated as [?], in place of saying, “They will be purified in peace.” Having called the Life-giver heavenly, he then foretells his care in the flesh by calling him a mountain: “A mountain of God, a fertile mountain.” He changed the name “Heavenly One” to the name “mountain”—not that he himself changed in his true nature, but according to his saving work he likewise gathers these names together in his own person. Our Life-giver is called God, Lord, Creator, Almighty, Heavenly One, King, and Mountain. The blessed prophet Isaiah speaks of this mountain: “In the last days,” says the Lord, “the mountain of the Lord and the house of God will be manifest above the tops of the mountains.” “And many nations will go and say, ‘Come, let us go to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob.’ For laws will go out from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem, and he will judge among many nations.”

The blessed Daniel also glorifies this mountain beforehand, when he interprets the statue composed of various kinds of materials, which stood fashioned from gold, silver, bronze, iron, and clay. And at the end he says, “A stone was cut out without hands, struck the statue and crushed it, and the stone became a great [?] mountain and filled the whole world.” See how certain things stated in detail do not agree with spiritual interpretations. For if he were speaking of a visible mountain when he said, “The stone became a great mountain and filled the world,” the filling indicates some beneficial effect. But when a mountain extends over everything, it does not fill but covers. It is clear that he calls the Life-giver’s saving work a mountain, because it is higher than every beneficial means, surpassing the law and the prophets, and those who spoke of God and wrote the praises. “It will rise above all the hills,” he says. And here too the Life-giver, speaking about the church, says to the apostles, “A city standing on a mountain cannot be hidden.” What city? The church: “Jerusalem, built as a city.” The prophet also calls it a house above the tops of the mountains. What house? The church. But be careful, lest we speak of other things and do violence to the truth. Let us also look at testimony appropriate to this, showing that the church is indeed called a house. Listen to Paul, who writes to Timothy: “So that you may know how you ought to conduct yourself in the house of God, which is the church of the living God.” And if the Church is the house of the living God, then the prophet rightly said, “The house of God is above the tops of the mountains.” This means that the Church is above every height. And many nations will go to the house, for many nations do not make their way to the Jewish [?], but to the Church. And they will say, “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob.” We have said many times who the God of Jacob is, according to the meaning of the passage: the God of Jacob appeared as God and man.

And now the blessed David says, “When the heavenly one scatters the kings upon it, it will be covered with snow on Zalmon: a mountain of God, a rich mountain.” He calls the Life-giver’s work of salvation a rich mountain, meaning that it is abundant, strong, and covered with every kind of flower. For “rich” indicates the ability to produce every kind of flower, as he also says in one place, “The beauty of the wilderness will flourish abundantly,” and again, “These are the sons of abundance.” He calls it a curdled mountain. It gathers and makes firm what is scattered, fluid, and watery, just as rennet gathers and thickens the fluid substance of milk. And it brings what is loose and dispersed into a single unity. After that, it cannot be separated from that with which it was united: neither the one from the other, nor the other from the one. In the same way, Christ, once he has united with our spirits like rennet with milk, is not separated or dissolved. Such was Paul’s spirit as well. It was once fluid like milk, but after it was united with Christ, he said, “Who will separate us from the love of Christ?” “A mountain of God, a rich mountain, a curdled mountain.” He calls the Life-giver a rich mountain, just as the Scriptures also call the prophets mountains. “His foundations,” he says, “are on the holy mountains.” And in another place he likewise says, “You wonderfully give light to the everlasting mountains.” He calls the prophets everlasting mountains. This accords with the saying, “Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel, for he has visited and brought salvation to his people, as he spoke through the mouths of the prophets who were from ancient times.” And for this reason, “You wonderfully illuminate the everlasting mountains.” “His foundations”—whose? The Life-giver’s—“are on the holy mountains,” for the foundations of this proclamation of the gospel are the prophetic writings. For this very reason, the apostle makes the statement still clearer and says, “You are the temple of the living God, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, whose cornerstone is Jesus Christ.” And the prophets are called mountains for this reason: just as a mountain comes from the earth and rises above the earth in height, being from it yet above it, so the prophets, because they were from among human beings yet above human beings, were called mountains. The Life-giver too is called a mountain, for he is related to them according to the flesh, but in his divinity he surpasses all flesh and every human mind. And because the prophets were called mountains and the Life-giver a mountain, people supposed that he was one of the prophets, as he himself says, “Who do people say that I, the Son of Man, am?” And they say, “Some say John the Baptist, some Jeremiah, some Elijah, and some one of the prophets.” And they thought that the holy mountain was one of the prophets. The blessed David says beforehand, “Why do you, curdled mountains, have such thoughts about the mountain in which God was pleased to dwell?” “Who do people say the Son of Man is?” They answered and said, “Some say Jeremiah, some Elijah, and some John the Baptist.” Do you see how the prophet speaks beforehand of their suppositions? “Why,” he says, “do you consider the mountain in which God was pleased to dwell to be curdled mountains?” And how did he dwell there? For he did not dwell in the prophets in this way, as it also says here: “The Lord will dwell in it forever.” There he took lodging for a time, but here he has an everlasting dwelling.

And pay attention to the sequence, how Scripture shows that the same one is heavenly, the same one is the mountain, the same one is also God, and the same one is also the Savior of the universe: the same one, the one who appeared in the world. For it says, “The Lord will dwell forever,” and then, “The chariots of God are ten thousandfold.” First it called him heavenly, then a mountain, and then God: “The chariots of God are ten thousandfold, thousands of drivers, and the Lord is among them at Sinai, in holiness. He ascended on high, took captivity captive.” The prophet speaks of [?], whose chariots are ten thousandfold, with thousands of drivers: “He ascended on high, took captivity captive, and gave gifts to the children of humankind.” And Paul, taking up the prophet’s intention, [?] brings it into the meaning of the gospel: “To each one grace has been given according to the measure of Christ’s gift.” He also adds the prophet’s testimony to this, for it expressly says, “He ascended on high.” Who is the God who ascended, whose chariots are ten thousandfold, with a thousand drivers? Who could it be who ascended? The one of whom he said, “When the heavenly one scattered the kings over them.” For he says, “He ascended on high and took captivity captive.” He sets out the saying and explains it himself: “What does ‘he ascended’ mean,” he says, “except that he first descended into the lower parts of the earth? The one who descended is the same one who ascended above the heavens.” The prophet says that he gave gifts to humankind, and the apostle explains who gave the gifts: “The one who ascended above the heavens,” he says, “is the one who gave.” Just as it says there that he gave, so also here: “Some as apostles, some as prophets, some as evangelists.” See the abundance of his divinity! See the authority of the glorious one’s glories! “He gave,” it says. He did not ask, but gave.

“He ascended on high and took captivity captive.” What captivity was there on high? Here he calls the cross “on high,” in accordance with the saying, “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up.” Thus it is clear that they call the cross “on high,” for on the cross he drew to himself all human beings, whom Satan had held in exile as captives. For this reason he calls the cross “on high,” because on the cross he broke the tyranny of the tyrants and brought back the captives, in accordance with the saying, “You shall call the captives to freedom.” Christ took those same captives captive. Satan took them captive in one way, and Christ in another: Satan took them from freedom into slavery, but Christ from slavery into freedom, from unbelief into belief. And because the custom had already taken hold, and the very name of captivity was dreadful, the world thought that it would be taken captive through the violence of some tyrant. For it did not know the truth and prepared for battle against the gospel. But the Giver of Life, concealing the intention of his love for humanity, advanced in battle array and sent flashes of lightning against his enemies. He rains arrows down from the bow of the Spirit, in accordance with what the apostle says: “The weapons of our warfare are not fleshly, but powerful for tearing down fortified arguments and every proud thing raised up against the knowledge of Christ; and we take every thought captive into obedience to Christ.” And because his love for humanity overpowered [?] captivity, and the world thought that he ascended to the heights on the cross, he took captivity captive and gave gifts to people. When people take captives, they seize possessions. But the one skilled in the great King's taking of captives, holding fast to love for humanity, took nothing from the captives; instead, he even gave to them.

Paul was like this. He once took captives while he was deceived by [?], and afterward he was taken captive by the power of Christ. And he acknowledged this good captivity. “Mark, my beautiful one, greets you,” he says. He turned away from bitter captivity and entered holy captivity. And the Life-giver led him about in the bonds of the gospel, as a spectacle and an example, not to humiliate him, but to make him glorious. And he considered captivity so pleasant that he even boasted of the bonds of his captivity. And listen to him: “I appeal to you, I, Paul, grown old, but now also a prisoner of Jesus Christ.” And elsewhere, with chains upon him, he said, “It is because of the hope of Israel that I wear these chains.” And he writes to Timothy, “Share in suffering for the gospel, for which I too suffer in bonds as though I were a criminal.” But look at the boldness of that noble soul: “But the word of God,” he says, “is not bound. I endure everything for the chosen, so that they may emulate me.”

Do you see what kind of captivity he took captive? “He ascended,” it says, “to the heights and took captivity captive.” From whom? From Satan. For human bodies were vessels of Satan, and vessels of many different kinds. And just as in a house one vessel is for oil, another for wine, another for vinegar, and another vessel is made of iron or some other material, and all belong to one master, so Satan took humanity and made vessels of many different kinds: some vessels of sexual immorality, some of adultery, some of deceit, some of oppression, some of greed, some of godlessness, some of blasphemy, some of confused speech, and some of dishonor. The Life-giver came and saw that all had been seized. He said to the disciples, “No one can enter a strong man's house and seize his [?].” He calls Satan strong—not because he was at all strong in comparison with him, but in comparison with the people who fought against him. “Unless he first binds the strong man, and then seizes his vessels.” Do you see that the Life-giver too seized those who had been seized and took captive those who had been taken captive?

And indeed, he did what he said. For nowhere do you find that the Life-giver set his hand to the work of teaching people, or set forth the particulars of the word of truth, or drew anyone onto the paths of salvation, without first binding the slanderer. When he accepted the life-giving baptism that purifies everyone, and mixed the good leaven—his own holiness—with the water, and placed himself under the water, so that he might conceal the power of the leaven beneath the water, he was baptized and immediately went from the Jordan into the wilderness to be tempted by Satan. Pay close attention to this, I beg you: how it agrees with this saying, “No one can seize the strong man's vessels unless he first binds the strong man.” Nowhere is the Savior seen teaching or performing any signs before he first bound Satan in the wilderness, and with him all his wickedness. Then, returning from the wilderness, he began with the divine teachings and seized those who had been seized by Satan—not through his divine power, but through his ministry in the flesh. For this was precisely his aim: to defeat Satan in the flesh, and not through his divinity. For it would have been a shameful battle and victory if God entered into combat with Satan. But, as I have said many times, because the enemy’s struggle was against human beings, he arms human nature in himself against the adversary, so that it may wound the one who wounded it.

And now, having taken from him the vessels—that is, human souls, which had gone astray and stumbled, wandering amid every kind of evil— he then sends these human souls, withered by every kind of evil, as his own instruments against the very adversary from whom he took them. Paul the persecutor was also a vessel of evil [?], an abuser and an opponent of God. For he was fighting against God when he fought against Christ [?]. “Whoever denies the Son,” he says, “also dishonors the Father.” Notice how the apostle himself also tears down his former ignorance. “This saying is trustworthy,” he says, “that Jesus Christ came into the world to save sinners, of whom I myself am the foremost.” He takes the opponent of God, the zealot for the law who unknowingly waged war against Christ, the vessel full of ignorance and zeal, and makes him a chosen instrument. And listen to him himself saying to Ananias, “Go, for he is a chosen instrument for me.” Do you see how he made a chosen instrument out of a vessel of evil? Elsewhere Paul also calls human beings vessels. “If God wished,” he says, “to show his wrath and make his power known, he endured with great patience the vessels of wrath.” He calls the souls of unbelievers vessels of wrath: “so that he might show the greatness of his mercy upon the vessels of mercy, which he prepared beforehand”—us, the instruments of mercy. He speaks of those who became worthy of his loving kindness and became chosen instruments. And this is precisely what is meant by, “He ascended on high and took captivity captive.” He himself also points to the same thing. “When I am lifted up,” he says—that is, when I go up onto the cross—“I will draw [?] everyone to myself.” So he brought those who had been seized to himself and brought back the captives. He freed the exiles and healed the afflicted. He broke the bonds with which sins had bound them, and in their place he put a crown on the heads of those who had been bound. And to learn that sins are bonds, listen to Scripture, which says, “Each person is bound in the cords of his own sins.” And because he found sins to be bonds, the Lamb of God, who took away the sins of the world, broke those sins. Oh, the loving kindness of our benefactor and Lord! When a master pursues a runaway slave and catches him, if he finds him free, he binds him; if he finds him healthy, he beats him; and if he finds him in the light, he shuts him in a dark prison. But the Savior pursued human nature, which had fled from truth and goodness, from the laws and the commandments. He found it not free but bound, and he freed it; naked, and he clothed it. “All of you,” he says, “who were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ.” He found everyone in prison and brought them out of prison; he found them in darkness and gave them light. “Land of Zebulun and Naphtali,” he says, “the road by the sea, beyond the Jordan: the people who sat in darkness saw a great light.”

And where did he find them bound and set them free? In the error of worshiping many gods, as though in a cistern and in a deep pit. And to learn that the cistern is the worship of idols, listen to the prophet Jeremiah: “The heavens were astonished,” he says, “and the earth shuddered, because the people committed two evils.” “They abandoned me,” he says, “the spring of living water, and dug leaky cisterns for themselves.” He calls himself a spring because a spring pours out water from its own sources, while a cistern holds water obtained from elsewhere and brought into it. And because they abandoned the true God and strayed toward false gods. And as Paul also says, “When you did not know God, you served those who were not gods by nature.” You stood bound in the pit of ignorance, in the dungeon of idolatry. Therefore David himself raises his lament and cries out, “Save me from those who go down into the pit.” Therefore the blessed Isaiah also says, “The people who sat in darkness saw a great light.” And to explain what darkness they were in, he adds, “The people who sat in darkness and the shadow of death.” And the other speaks of the Life-giver himself, saying, “By the blood of your covenant you released the prisoners from the waterless pit.” By “the blood of the covenant” he means the forgiveness of sins, and by “prisoners,” those like Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ—not from a waterless pit. And how is it “by the blood of the covenant”? It is precisely this: “This is my blood of the new covenant, poured out for you for the forgiveness of sins.”

And pay careful attention. David says, “He ascended on high and took captivity captive, and gave gifts to people.” And all the prophets must speak in agreement, because one Spirit was in them all. This one says, “You released the prisoners from the waterless pit.” And another says, “Let them rejoice before you, as people rejoice in the days of summer.” Those who have been released, he says, should rejoice as in summertime. Therefore the Savior himself also said, “The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few. Ask the Lord of the harvest to send workers out to work in his harvest.” In this way, he says, those you have saved will rejoice, like those who rejoice at the harvest, gathering the fruits of their labors, or like those who divide the plunder. Warriors take much plunder in battle: gold, silver, and clothing. Everything a man has is called plunder, because it all lies scattered and in disorder, mixed together, the clothing, the weapons and the sword, the gold and silver and bread, and whatever else there may be. Likewise, Satan had taken everyone and mixed them together. Christ came and snatched them all together away from him—the drunkards, the greedy, and the robbers. For this reason he says, “Let them rejoice before you, as people rejoice in summertime, and as those who divide the plunder.” As David also says, “I will rejoice in your words like someone who finds much plunder.”

See these wonders: just as someone who wins a victory [?] binds the rebels and rescues those captured by the rebel, and the rebel always pictures death before his eyes, while the exiles rejoice because they have been released from tyranny and have come into the kingdom. Yet both the rebel who is to die and those who are to be freed are paraded as a spectacle because of the king’s victory. Likewise, the Life-giver captured Satan and the demons in battle, along with those who had been captured by him, and parades them together as a spectacle. And Paul speaks of both: “Christ,” he says, “is our peace, who made both one.” And he broke down the dividing barrier of the fence, the hostility, in his flesh, and removed the law of commandments with its ordinances. He annulled and removed the written decree that stood against us and nailed it to the cross. He stripped the authorities and powers and openly exposed them to shame. Just as people attach some token of victory to a pole—a helmet, armor, or some other remnant of the slain—and parade it around. Likewise, he bound Satan’s weapons to a royal standard and publicly disgraced the demons on the cross. But the demons are put on public display and kept in custody. Those who were carried off captive are also first put on public display, and afterward they go free. And listen to Paul: “Thanks,” he says, “to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ and spreads through us the fragrance of the knowledge of himself.” The rebel is put on public display, and we who were with the rebel are also put on public display, so that it may be clear who won, who the rebel was, and who was with the rebel. And because he captured the one and is going to kill him, but rescued and freed the others, these too must be put on public display for a time together with the one who is condemned to death and is going to his death. And concerning such people, who are to be put on public display and held captive, Isaiah says: “The toil [?] of the land of the Egyptians, and the merchants of the Ethiopians, and the Sabeans, men of great stature, will come to you and follow behind you, bound in shackles, and will offer prayers to you.” This shows that they come into captivity not for destruction, but for relief. “They will follow behind you,” he says, “bound in shackles, and will stand before you in prayer, because God is in you, and there is no God except in you.”

The demons are put on public display, and the apostles are also put on public display: the former are struck with shame at their defeat, while the latter proclaim the King’s victory. The demons were put on public display then; heretics are also put on public display now, acting as enemies while presenting themselves as members of the household. Just as war within a household is worse than any other war, so the error of heretics is worse than every other error. If a pagan insults Christ in any way, I do not consider it strange, because he is an enemy of the cross. I say nothing of the Jew, because he is plainly an enemy. But the heretic who pretends to confess Christ and denies Christ, who undertakes to preach the Holy Spirit and blasphemes the Holy Spirit—this warfare distresses me like warfare within a household. Just as fighting within a city is worse than any other fighting, so turmoil within a house is more bitter than any fighting within a city. And worse than turmoil in a city or a house is the turmoil between husband and wife; and still more terrible is the smoke that rises between [?] and [?]. And still worse is the turmoil between [?] and the stepchildren. Consider hostility within a household. Picture [?] the man who comes home from the marketplace and faces a winter storm [?]. When it is time for the meal and for rejoicing, he instead finds himself in a battle. Cares and sorrows multiply and make the harbors storm-tossed. At home they are tossed about as though at sea; they leave the house and hurry to the marketplace as though to a harbor. God-fearing men endured such conflicts for Christ’s sake. Christ spoke of them when he said: “Brother will hand over brother to death, and a father his son, and children will rise against their fathers.” “A son will be divided from his father, and a father from his son, a mother from her daughter, a mother-in-law from her daughter-in-law, and a daughter-in-law from her mother-in-law; and the master of the house will have his own household members as his enemies.” Just as war within a house is more terrible than any other war, so the error of heretics is worse than every other error. They seem to share the same household ties and the same profession of devotion to God, clothed in the outward appearance of devotion to God, yet they fight against the truth. Paul says of them: “They have the outward form of truth, but have denied its power.”

And now, if we say the same thing, let no one be displeased by it, for the concern is not that we should say only new things, but whether we can say something true, saying the same thing and explaining it differently. Even if the meaning is consistent, the word has many forms of interpretation. God too is one, and he spoke in many portions and in many ways to our fathers, the prophets, and to the apostles. We do not shrink from the former or the latter because the same Holy Spirit spoke in both; rather, we see one power and various workings. And when the Father speaks in the prophets, the Son speaks; and when the Son speaks in the apostles, the Father speaks. And when the Holy Spirit speaks in the prophets and the apostles, the Father and the Son speak. There are no divisions there, nor any cutting apart of the indivisible nature, nor any dividing of the undivided kingdom.

Do you wish to know how it is undivided? Listen to the one who spoke to Moses when he was reluctant to go to the land of the Egyptians. “I am not capable,” he says, “of entering Pharaoh’s house, for I have a weak voice and a heavy tongue. I beg you, Lord, take someone else in hand.” When he saw that hesitation arising from weakness was resisting the command of the one who commanded, he showed him who the craftsman was and who was able to fashion the bodily organ. He says, “Who gave a mouth to a human being? Or who made those who see and those who are blind? Was it not I, the Lord? I gave everyone a mouth, and I can give one to you. “I who bestowed this on everyone—shall I deprive you, my prophet, of these gifts? Who gave a mouth to a human being? Was it not I, the Lord God?” And to Ezekiel he says, “Son of man, behold, I will raise up a horn for the whole house of Israel, and I will give you an open mouth.” It is not that he was giving him a mouth, which he had from birth; rather, he calls boldness a mouth. And let us seek this in the Gospel: who gives the mouth? “When they bring you before tribunals,” he says, “do not worry about what you will say, for I will give you a mouth and wisdom.” And it is clear that the one who said to Moses, “Who gave human beings a mouth?” also says to Ezekiel, “I will give you a mouth.” But he himself is the one who spoke in ancient times, worked in the prophets, and placed his power in the apostles.

Again, Scripture speaks of lips—not visible lips, but boldness—when David says, “Lord, if you open my lips,” not because his lips were closed, but because he is asking for the boldness he had lost. And how could he even have said that very thing: “Lord, if you open my lips”? And in the Old Testament, before one language had been confused into many languages, Moses wanted to show that there was one speech and one language. And he says, “The whole earth was one lip.” Did all human beings have only one lip? Surely he called the single speech of their mouths “one lip.” “The whole earth,” he says, “was one lip and one speech.” And it is clear that everyone spoke the same language.

“I,” he says, “will give a mouth and wisdom.” And where do we find that he gave them? If we find that he gave them to one person, then we will not doubt concerning the others. “Some of the Cyrenians and Alexandrians arose,” it says, “and entered into questioning and debate with Stephen.” Remember: “For I will give you a mouth and wisdom, and they will not be able to oppose you.” And they could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit by which he spoke. See how God gives a mouth to the prophets, Christ opens the mouths of the apostles, and the Holy Spirit speaks in them.

But lest anyone suppose that the Son gives and the Spirit brings about the effect—as though giving belonged to one and bringing about the effect to another—it is necessary to show that the Holy Spirit also gives. As it also says in the Old Testament that he gives, and in the Gospel Christ says to the apostles, “I will give you a mouth.” We must ask: is the one who gives different from the one who brings? Even now, when kings give gifts, their servants carry the gift; they are not counted as having the same standing. Let us see: does the Son perhaps give, while the Spirit acts as a servant and attendant? But so that you may learn that, just as the Son [?] the word to the prophets and apostles, so the Spirit also is not an attendant but gives abundantly, it says in the Acts of the Apostles: “When the Holy Spirit came down upon them, they spoke in various languages, as the Spirit gave them utterance.” Paul says, “One and the same Spirit works all these things and distributes to each person as he himself wills.” As he wills, and not as he receives a command. And again, to show that what he himself gives is also the gift of the Holy Spirit, and that what he himself [?] is also the working of the Spirit, the Savior says to the apostles: “When they bring you before the courts, do not worry about what you will say, for it is not you who will speak, but the Holy Spirit will teach you at that very hour what you should say.” Do you see that where the Father works, there is the working of the Son and the abundance of the Holy Spirit?

Where there is teaching and illumination and discourse about the worship of God, no created nature is found at work there, but only the uncreated nature. Whether in the illumination of baptism, or in the ineffable mysteries, it is not within an angel’s authority to illuminate and sanctify, but within the sovereign authority of the holy and uncreated nature. When he speaks through the prophets, it is not any created nature that speaks, but the uncreated [?], according to the saying, “As he spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets, who were from of old.” But when someone is to be delivered from afflictions, God sends angels. Whether to deliver someone from lions or to save someone from fire, angels become servants of such deliverance. As Paul also says, “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent to serve those who are to inherit salvation?” But the Holy Spirit appears when the mysteries are to be performed, when the abundance of teaching is to be bestowed, and when the ineffable mysteries of baptism are to be accomplished.

And let receiving sanctification through water and the Spirit in no way trouble your mind. For they say, “If the uncreated nature comes for the illumination of baptism, what need is there for water, which is created? And why,” they say, “did the Savior join the uncreated nature to the created nature?” He says, “Unless you are baptized in water and the Spirit, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.” And who does not know that water is created? But it is necessary to explain on what grounds and for what purpose created water is joined to the uncreated Spirit. I beg you, do not grow weary of listening, and gather the meaning of these words of mine into the storehouses of your minds, so that they do not flow uselessly past your ears. Just as water spread over the ground does not enter the earth or give the fields drink, but when it enters a channel and runs through the furrows, it is not wasted on the ground but irrigates the fields, so now let my words not be scattered, but let the meaning of my words irrigate the fields of your minds.

God gave many things to human beings, and he himself has no need of what he gave. But because our mortal nature cannot receive the invisible gifts, he makes it familiar with such things through visible means. The Giver of Life could have granted forgiveness of sins without water, and the manifestation of the Spirit would have been enough to wash the one who was bound, cleanse the filthy, purify the defiled, and bring the exile into adoption as a child. But because human nature [?] something of these visible things, although it is weak and very limited in receiving divine things with the eyes of the mind, he leads it there by some easy outward means, for the sake of those who cannot rise so high and see invisible things. He set before them a visible example, so that through the clear certainty of their eyes their invisible souls might gain assurance. For example, when God took blessed Aaron, the brother of Moses, into the priesthood for himself, he said, “Clothe him in a flower-patterned robe woven from a mixture of threads, made of purple, scarlet, fine linen, and blue.” Blue, scarlet, and purple are known to everyone. As for fine linen, it is white like linen cloth. From materials of these four colors they fashioned the priceless robe. Gold and precious stones were inlaid in it, and there was a priestly turban on his head and a gold plate on his forehead, which bears the image of the Holy Spirit. On the priest’s belt were twelve precious stones: sardius, topaz, and emerald; carbuncle, sapphire, and jasper; jacinth, agate, and amethyst; chrysolite, beryl, and onyx. God commanded that all twelve stones be set in place: in the first row, the sardius, topaz, and emerald; in the second, the carbuncle, sapphire, and jasper; in the third, the jacinth, agate, and amethyst; and in the fourth, the chrysolite, beryl, and onyx. He commanded that the names of the tribes of Israel be inscribed on each of the stones: on the first, the name of the tribe of Reuben; on the second, that of the tribe of Simeon; on the third, that of the tribe of Levi; and those of all the others likewise, one by one. He commanded that the belt be placed around the priest’s waist, and that the ephod, made of scarlet, fine linen, purple, and blue, cover his shoulders and be divided across his chest. “Place two stones on the shoulders,” he said, “one on the right and one on the left. Inscribe the names of six tribes on one, and those of the other six on the other.” Why did he command that the names of the sons of Israel be inscribed twice? Was it not enough to have them on the shoulders alone, but also on the chest? Because of their wavering minds, he commanded it twice. Again, he spoke of pomegranate-shaped flowers at the neckline of the robe, and commanded the priest to enter the outer holy places dressed in this way.

God commanded all this because of their ignorance, so that at least through such splendor they might regard the holy places with awe. But the priest’s honor is not purple, scarlet, fine linen, or blue, but righteousness, as David himself says: “Let your priests be clothed in righteousness.” But because the garment of righteousness is visible only to the eyes of the mind, and God’s purpose is not merely to give further benefit to those who are perfect, but also to save everyone alike, when they see the majestic priest arrayed in divine splendor, they will call to mind that he is the priest of the great God. And to show that such a robe was made not because it was needed for the service of God, but to impress those who saw it, and that he has no need of it, but seeks sincerity of soul, And whoever has the virtues blossoming within him rejoices in purity of heart, for that itself is royal purple and the flower of faith. He gave Moses a command that when Aaron enters the Holy of Holies, he should take off the robe made of fine linen and scarlet, purple, and blue material, and put on a linen robe and enter the sanctuary. Where one sees God, there is no need for outward appearances or elaborate robes. Even the robe that he himself ordered to be made for other purposes, he commanded him to take off. But so that he should not dishonor the sanctuary by the nakedness of his body, he commands him to wear a linen robe and linen shoes—what is plain and without elaborate robes. For this reason he seeks what is plain, because that pleases God, not finery. Yet, brothers, although he gave Aaron the robe so that those who saw him would honor him, he also places in it a pattern of things to come, so that nothing should be entirely without meaning, and so that he might enlighten the hearts of those who would come afterward. The blessed Aaron takes that robe and puts on the whole world at once as though it were a tunic. For the world, too, is established from four elements: earth, fire, water, and air. From the earth comes the finest linen—from the peaceful earth—and from the sea comes the purple. The scarlet resembles fire, and the blue resembles air, for the air often turns blue. But let anyone understand this however he wishes, provided that he does so with a mind devoted to God.

But let us consider what lies before us: why he ordered the names to be engraved on the stones [?]. For the priest would enter before the altar, while the people stood outside and did not dare approach. It was a cause of sorrow that only one entered and enjoyed the sanctuary, while everyone else stood outside. Through the inscribed gems, God provides a means of consolation for their troubled minds. "You cannot enter by yourself," he says, "but I will carry you in through the names inscribed on the gems." The priest entered, bearing the twelve tribes, and presented them all to God. The priest's task is to present the people to God, for he is a mediator between God and human beings. He receives blessings from God and gives them to the people, and he takes prayers from the people and presents them to God. "The Lord said to Moses," it says, "Go down and warn the people." See how he acts as a mediator from God to human beings and conveys God's messages to the people. Again it says that Moses brought the people's prayers up to God and brought God's messages to the people. For this reason, when the prophet Malachi explained the priestly office, he said, "The lips of a priest declare knowledge, and people should seek the law from his mouth, for he is an angel of the Lord Almighty." He is called an angel, not because he has the nature of angels. Scripture calls the bearer of messages an angel. And angels are called angels because they declare God's will to the world. The name "angel" is not a name for their nature, but for their service. And because the name is shared, when Saul sent men to the prophet, it says, "He sent angels to tell him the king's affairs." And elsewhere it says that David sent angels to Abigail, Nabal's wife, to tell her David's intentions.

But the matter before us is to show that the priest was a mediator, that he brought the people to God, and that he bore the people's weakness. Whoever offers a sacrifice offers it holding it against his breast, for these are the distinctive signs of those who present offerings. And whoever bears weakness bears it on his shoulders. For this reason he inscribes the names of the people on the priest’s shoulders, to teach the priest that you who are strong must bear the weakness of the weak. Paul also says this: You who are strong, bear the weakness of the weak. And that priest was a figure of Christ. Through their names he bore the twelve tribes of Israel—the entire people. But Christ bears still more in his body: the whole world. He also carries it against his breast, for he himself gave humanity rest upon his breast. And to learn that he also bears humanity on his shoulders, listen to the Lord’s own parable. He says: Which of you, having a hundred sheep, if one of them goes astray, will not leave the ninety-nine sheep in the mountains and go and seek the one that has strayed? If he finds it, truly I tell you, he will also place it on his shoulders. For this reason the giver of life also carries the cross on his shoulders, because through it he bore the entire world. And Jesus went out, it says, carrying the cross on his shoulders. And why on his shoulders? So that Isaiah would not prove false when he said: A child was born to us, and a son was given, whose authority is upon his shoulders. The priest carries it in [?] and on his shoulders, for the priest’s task is to present the people and bear the people’s weakness. But let us return to the matter before us.

We made mention of explaining why water is joined with the Spirit. Just as there a robe fashioned with flowers of various kinds was given to the priest, although God had no need of the flowers’ various colors, so that it might delight the eyes of those who were under instruction, and through visible glory they might be encouraged toward invisible things. Likewise our God, knowing that the nature of the Spirit is uncreated, mingled the adorned nature with the uncreated nature, so that the eyes of the ignorant, looking into the water, might see the Holy Spirit as they see the sun in water. Do you not know that those who cannot look directly at the sun look into water and see the whole [?]? You have not seen for yourself; at least see through this water. And from this very point you find that the apostles were not baptized with water. But let them not quibble pointlessly; instead, listen to the explanation to its conclusion. For the apostles, because they were perfect and received perfection even before the cross of the giver of life, were not baptized in water; rather, the grace of the Holy Spirit was sufficient for them.

But the opponents immediately object. They say: They were baptized, and the Savior bears witness to this. When he heard Peter say, Not only my feet, but also my head, he said to him: One who has been washed does not need washing. And it is clear that he had received baptism. And they do not understand that he called the apostles’ baptism not water, but the word. You, he says, are already clean because of the word that I have spoken to you. And that by “washed” he means not someone baptized with water, but someone enlightened by the word, is clear from this: before his sufferings he says, One who has been washed does not need washing. And after his sufferings, the cross, and the resurrection, when he was about to ascend, the disciples gathered together and asked him: Lord, when will you establish the kingdom of Israel? He said to them: It is not for you to know the times or the hours that the Father has set by his own authority, but you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you. And what does he say after that? “John baptized,” he says, “in water, but you will be baptized.” He did not say, “You have been baptized.” He said this after the resurrection, and before the resurrection he spoke of “the one who has washed.” For if they had been baptized before the passion, he would not have said to those already enlightened, “You will be baptized in the Holy Spirit not many days from now.” And how was it “not many days from now”? For when forty days after the resurrection were completed, he ascended, and ten days later, when Pentecost had come, the Holy Spirit appeared. And the giver of life said much the same thing: “You will be baptized not many days from now”—that is, after ten days. “You,” he says, “will be baptized in the Holy Spirit.” He did not say “in water,” but “in the Spirit,” for participation in the Spirit alone is sufficient for perfecting and sanctifying. “When he came,” he says, “the Holy Spirit arrived and filled the house where they were sitting.” There was no water anywhere there. This was to make clear that where divine power appears, there is no need for an act or material substance. Rather, the Spirit is sufficient to accomplish enlightenment even without water.

But God does not wish the tradition of the mysteries to be dishonored on the grounds of perfection, lest you say, “Since I am able to attain it in my mind, what need is there for baptism in water?” And our aim in this is to show that God is able to give the gifts of grace even without water. He is able to enlighten even without water, but we are not able to receive enlightenment without water. And since the Savior’s instruction took place for our teaching, we must bear in mind that, even if we are perfect, no one is more perfect than Christ. The giver of life wished to remove every excuse, so as not to leave you a pretext for avoiding the water. He himself was therefore baptized first in the Jordan River. But let us return to the matter before us.

When the Spirit rests upon someone, he baptizes that person, even if that person has not yet been baptized in water. And I do not mean only the apostles. In the house of Cornelius too, when Peter spoke, while he was still speaking, the Spirit came and rested upon Cornelius and his household. And this was not without purpose. Rather, the Holy Spirit knew that Peter’s mind was troubled by scruples and that he hesitated to baptize those who were Gentiles. For at that time the apostles thought that Christ’s grace had been given only to the Jewish people. They shrank from giving baptism to those who were Gentiles and had scruples about doing so. The divine Spirit wished to show that human minds cannot prevent this gift. He rested upon them before baptism, before they were instructed and enrolled. When Peter saw that the Spirit had descended and rested upon them, he said, “Can I withhold water from these people, who have already received the Holy Spirit, just as we did, without water?” Again, this same Peter explained the circumstances to the apostles who were in Jerusalem, for they took issue with him and said, “You ate and drank with Gentiles.” And Peter set out his answer in order and laid it before them, saying, “I was in the city of Joppa, and they summoned me there. While I was speaking the word to them, the Holy Spirit came and rested upon them. And I remembered the Lord’s words, which he spoke: ‘John baptized in water, but you were baptized in the Holy Spirit.’”

Do you see how water has been given as a necessary means of reassuring human minds? For even the person who is to be enlightened is twofold: [?] of body and soul. And the nature of the soul is invisible, while the body's structure is visible. God gave a twofold gift to both parts: water, openly, to the visible body, and the invisible gift of the Holy Spirit, secretly, to the human soul. And just as royal gifts are bestowed through both living hands and lifeless instruments—for the reed pen and the ink are lifeless tools, while the king's hand is living— the reed pen and ink are not equal in honor to the king's hand merely because the king's hand needs the reed pen and ink. Likewise, although water is needed, like ink, so that the divine writing may be imprinted through visible water, is water equal in honor to the Spirit? Rather, we must understand that the Holy Spirit writes his benevolence with water. Often people presented letters of petition to kings. While the letter is still in the hands of those presenting it, it is called a letter of petition. But when the king puts his hand to it, it is called a document granting gifts. Before the king adds his signature, it is a sheet of paper, worth only ten small coins. But when the king puts his hand to it and confirms it, it is worth many measures of gold, and what was inexpensive becomes valuable. What sold for little is sold for a great price. Although it is received free of charge, the favor has shown the extent of the generosity. Just as the paper, ink, and reed pen in that case are worth little until the king has put his hand to it, and when the king confirms it, you no longer look at the paper and the reed pen, but at the gift from the hand of the king who wrote it, so too, when you see water by itself, [?] it is not worth even a single dang coin. But if you see the Spirit descending and resting upon the waters, you will understand that it is the invisible [?] of sovereign power, through the Lord's grace; and what is seen is water, the instrument of invisible gifts of grace.

For this reason there is water—not so that it may be counted alongside the Spirit, but so that it may lead you to the invisible. Where the nature of the one who calls people to himself is invisible, a visible mediator is needed, so that through what is visible they may approach what is invisible. And I will bring forward an example from ancient times. The laws proclaimed God, but he was invisible, as God. He gave laws, so that they might not [?] through visible laws, but he was invisible, as God. He gave laws, so that they might not learn about invisible things while despising the visible laws. Moses becomes a mediator between God and human beings, so that those who cannot see God may look upon Moses' face and through him see the invisible. Moses is joined to God, not as someone equal in honor, but as a mortal who, through his face, becomes a guide to the immortal nature. They believed in God together with Moses, and in Moses, and in Moses together with God. But they ought not to have believed in Moses without God, for no one believed in a human being; nor ought they to have believed in God without Moses, for without a mediator mortal nature could not lead the way. For this reason, the blessed Paul says that the law was given, ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator. And Moses was the mediator between God and the people.

And see the remarkable thing: Scripture says that the people believed in God and in Moses his servant. Surely Moses is not equal in honor to God merely because it said that the people believed in God and in Moses? Even if Moses is counted alongside God, he is not equal in honor to the Holy Spirit. Elsewhere Scripture says that all the people feared God and Samuel. Does the statement that they also feared Samuel mean that Samuel is equal in honor to God? Rather, they feared the one as Lord and the other as a mediator. Likewise, when you hear of the mystery of water and the Spirit, consider in your mind the abundance of the Spirit [?], as true gifts, as uncreated grace, as an everlasting kingdom. When you see the water, recognize that the visible serves as a mediator to the invisible and divine nature. This accords with the statements that the people believed Moses and God, and feared the Lord and Samuel. Elsewhere it says, “The sword of the Lord and of Gideon.” For Gideon was their commander, and God their protector. It says, “The sword of the Lord and of Gideon”: of the one as king, and of the other as mediator.

I say all this so that you do not bring these ideas together carelessly and indiscriminately, failing to understand the different aspects of the meanings of the words and the things. Those who put such words, names, and ranks together are like people mixing various [?] materials together, as someone might mix gold, silver, iron, copper, and lead together. Likewise, someone whose thoughts are confused and who cannot distinguish things from one another is not acceptable, even if he offers a sacrifice. As God himself also says, “If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, you have sinned. Its turning shall be toward you.” One must not merely offer rightly, but also divide rightly. What does dividing mean? To understand the authority of the Spirit and also recognize the mediating role of the water. But if you mix everything together—Moses and God, Samuel and the Lord, water and the Holy Spirit—you will then find various [?] materials mixed together. As God himself also says, “Son of man, the house of Israel has mixed copper, lead, and iron. Therefore say: Because they have mixed gold, silver, iron, and lead together, behold, I will receive you as into a smelting furnace and melt you down for purification, so that you will no longer be mixed together.”

“But,” they say, “we do not find the Holy Spirit to be a divine authority, but rather a gift of royal abundance. For it is written that the Holy Spirit is an anointing. It says, ‘Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit.’ Is the Spirit God? Look, he is an anointing. And just as the forms of the anointing are different from those of the people being anointed, so also,” they say, “God, who anointed, has one essence, and the Spirit, who is the anointing, has another nature.” And since the heretics seek merely to enumerate the [?], without examining their meanings, merely moving words back and forth and corrupting the order of worship with human reasoning, let us also give them an answer: “Look, you yourself say that the anointing has one nature and those being anointed another. You will also acknowledge that a fisherman has one nature and a fish another; a garment has one nature and a weaver another; shepherding has one nature and a sheep another; a cultivator has one nature and a vineyard another. Will not their respective masters appear distinct from one another? Then pay attention. The Savior says to the apostles, ‘Come after me, and I will make you fishers of people.’ The apostles are fishers, and those caught in their catch are people. And now the heretic will say: Just as the nature of fish is different from that of human beings, so the nature of human beings must be different from that of the apostles who preach. Just as the nature of the fisherman is different from that of the fish, so the nature of those who learn is different from that of those who teach. Who would accept such tangled, delirious words and not know that the teachers were from this world and the learners were human beings? The apostle also says: You are God's building, God's cultivated field. And do you not know that the nature of a building is different from that of its builder? And again: Like an architect, I laid a foundation. If Paul was an architect and they were a building, were the natures of the architect and the building different? If you follow only the words, see how far the error spreads. Again the apostle says: I planted, Apollos watered, but God made it grow. And here we see that those who plant belong to one order and those who water to another; and again, those who plant are different from the plant. Is the nature of Paul, who planted, different from the nature of the Corinthians, who were planted by him? Why do you stumble over the words and not look at the meaning? The Holy Spirit is called anointing, so that by a visible name he may proclaim invisible gifts of grace. For in former times kings were anointed with oil from a sacred horn, as were priests and prophets. But the Holy Spirit, who descended and rested upon the Life-Giver as an example, and not because of any need, appeared without oil. Afterward, too, he enlightened many without water and anointed many without oil. And pay attention, I beg you: when the Holy Spirit wishes to show his works, he anoints even without oil. From where did Moses receive the power to anoint Aaron, when he himself had not been anointed? But because Moses was perfect, he received the resting of the Holy Spirit without oil. For the Spirit was in Moses, and for that reason he had no need of oil. Likewise, the apostles baptized with water and the Spirit, though they themselves were not baptized with water, but with the Spirit. Likewise Moses, who had not been anointed with oil but with the Spirit, anointed Aaron with holy oil.

He is called anointing for many useful purposes. For the human race became sick, and disease seized the whole world. He came and found the entire world paralyzed. He anoints it to heal its nature of [?]. He anoints it to train it for battle against Satan. What oil is to an athlete in combat, the power of the Spirit is to those who contend against Satan. He calls the Spirit anointing to show that he restored this diseased and mortal nature to immortal glory.

He is also called a gift. For the heretics say that the Spirit is a gift of God, since Scripture itself says that God gave the Holy Spirit to those who submit to him. They say: The one who gives is different from the gift. If you call the Spirit a gift because he is given, then, if that is so, call the Son a gift as well, for the Son too was given. God so loved the world, it says, that he gave his Son. He gave the Spirit, and he gave the Son. Therefore both are gifts. Can you deny that the Son is God because he was called the Father's gift? Rather, he is a gift according to the divine plan, and God according to the honor belonging to his nature. And the Holy Spirit is God because of his authority, and a gift because of his participation in the mystery. For whatever is given is a gift; yet that gift is often also found to be a giver. God gave his only-begotten Son, and he was called a gift. Again, the gift itself is a gift: “He ascended,” it says, “on high, took captivity captive, and gave gifts to people.” He gave and was given. He gave as God and was given as man. But let this suffice on this subject.

I know that I have prolonged this discourse, not to gratify some thought of my own, but to stir up your longing. For you always long to see how the slander they cast upon the Holy Spirit may be cleared up, because you are friends of the Father, beloved of the Son, and devoted to the Holy Spirit. Do not be surprised that I call servants friends: servants because of their nature, and friends because of grace. And listen to the Lord himself: “I will no longer call you servants,” he says, “but friends.” The Lord [?] to call them friends, and should we shrink from doing so? For this same reason, Hananiah and his companions said, “Have mercy on us for the sake of Abraham your servant and Isaac your beloved.” And David said, “Your friends have become exceedingly precious to me, O God.”

Let us say this boldly; let every mouth proclaim this same thing. For the mouths of the prophets have been entrusted to us, even though we are not worthy of the prophets. The mouths of the apostles have been entrusted to us, even though we do not come close to the apostles. Nevertheless, let us not cast away the honor entrusted to us, but sharpen our tongues—not to slaughter unbelievers, but to turn their unbelief around and set it right. A bold mouth belonged especially to the prophets. A bold mouth was the particular possession of the apostles, who were firm pillars of the worship of God. Their mouths were open and never closed, as Paul also says: “Our mouths are open to you, Corinthians.” Open mouths: “I will give you,” he says, “an open mouth.” Our mouths too are open, for we are mouthpieces of orthodox praise against heretical error. They are open and do not close. Even if our words fall silent, their effects do not cease. For God knows those who will be saved; he recognizes those who will turn back. Just because those who speak do not know into whom their words enter, does God also fail to recognize those who will be caught?

The word of preachers is a net. Just as a fisherman spreads out his casting net and throws the net, the one who throws it knows that he has thrown it, but does not know what has been caught, because the tool does its work unseen in the depths of the waters. Likewise, when the casting net of the divine word is thrown into hidden souls, the speaker does not know who has fallen into the net. But God, who examines the net, knows which fish has been caught: which of those who fight against the Spirit the proclamation of the Spirit’s divinity has brought into the net, and which of the Arians the glories of Christ have drawn in. God stands and examines minds, and watches the work of the casting net. And to use yet another example: Just as those who cast the net stand apart from one another, with its ends spread out, and enclose the fish all around as though surrounding them with a wall, there is a hollow of water in the middle enclosed by the net. And when they wish to draw it in, the spread-out ends gradually approach one another, until the two sides of the net come together into one and its ends meet. Likewise, in the earlier, widely separated times, God appointed the prophets to cast the net, and in the second period, the apostles. The former cast the net with the old covenant, and the latter with the new. On the two sides, the two groups of net-casters enclose a single hollow between them. The hollow in the middle is the east, and opposite it are the west and the south. and opposite it, to the north. And hear the Lord himself: “They will come,” he says, “from east and west, from the north and from the sea, and will recline at table with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.” In that hollow, in that same pocket, fishermen catch fish for destruction, but these catch them for salvation. The two sides come together, and the net-casters are found to have one nature and one craft; those who were apart are joined together. So also at the end of this world, when the drawing of the net is complete [?], the prophets will come forward and show their labors—how much they drew in. And these will show their efforts—how much they brought under the net.

The same net is cast even now, but it is not drawn by our own hand; it is pulled by the apostolic right hand. And if I say anything from my own mind, do not accept it unless Paul says it, unless Isaiah bears witness to it. The hand of the prophets draws it, and now the right hand of the apostles stretches out the net. But there is also another example to observe. When a net is cast, the fish darts away and heads into the middle pocket. Often it even gets completely away from its adversary, like the disciples of the heretics now. And see the wonders: at first Satan cast a net over the world, and the demons drew it; but the righteous darted away and escaped beyond the net. As David also says, “By my God I will cross a wall.” Satan also cast a net from Babylon, so that he might cast everyone into [?]. And the three holy fish darted over the net with dry fins. And it is written that they said with the prophet, “Sinners will fall into his snares.” And because Satan cast an evil net over the world—the one who said, “I have wandered and traveled beneath heaven, and here I am”—Christ came and wove nets for him. Through the apostles he cast nets for those who had been caught by him, and brought the whole world under the net. What then? Are we inventing something from our own minds? Hear the Lord himself: “The kingdom of heaven is like a net that is cast into the sea and gathers from every side.” May all of us fall under that net and be found among its catch. And the wonder is this: the one who fell under the net today as a fish will tomorrow, as a fisherman, catch other fish. There, fish caught in the net go from life to death; here, those who fall under the net are gathered from death into life. That is why the Giver of Life says to Peter, “Cast your net on the right side.” And he gathered many fish. He teaches that through visible things we must reach an understanding of things perceived by the mind. For he also says to this same man, “Do not be afraid, Peter; from now on you will catch people for life.” This means that you will draw them into eternal life.

May all of us henceforth fall under the net of right belief, dwell in the holy bosom of faith, and carry within ourselves faith in the Trinity—the faith of the three patriarchs. For the heavenly Trinity is in heaven, and the three patriarchs are on earth. The nature of the one is not false, and honoring the other does not lead to denial. This trinity is divided by time and separated by places; but that one is timeless and eternal, always reigns, and saves [?], continually enlightens, and through it may all of us be saved in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory forever and ever.
